title: Divisibility Tests from Congruences
short: Since 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9) and 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11), digit sums and alternating digit sums test divisibility by 9 and by 11.
trouble: Students find a remainder mod 11 with the alternating sum started from the leftmost digit. That can give the negative of the true remainder; start with the ones digit.

blocks.html: You may know that a number is divisible by 9 when its digit sum is. With modular arithmetic this stops being a trick and becomes a two-line proof, and the same idea gives tests for 3, 11, 4, 8 and even 7 and 13.

Write $n = d_k 10^{k} + \cdots + d_1 10 + d_0$ in base 10. Since $10 \equiv 1 \pmod{9}$, every power $10^{i} \equiv 1$, so $$n \equiv d_k + \cdots + d_1 + d_0 \pmod{9}.$$ The same holds mod $3$. Since $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$, the powers $10^{0}, 10^{1}, 10^{2}, \dots$ are $\equiv 1, -1, 1, \dots$, so $$n \equiv d_0 - d_1 + d_2 - d_3 + \cdots \pmod{11},$$ with the signs starting at the ones digit.

head: Modulus

Test
blocks.cap: Each test is one congruence about a power of 10. They give the remainder, not just a yes or no.

blocks.title: Remainder mod 9
blocks.q: Find the remainder of $8{,}437{,}265$ divided by $9$.

blocks.title: A missing digit
blocks.q: The 6-digit number $7\square4312$ is divisible by 11. Find the missing digit.
steps: We need $\square - 7 \equiv 0 \pmod{11}$, and the only digit that works is $\square = 7$.

blocks.title: Blocks of three for 7
blocks.q: Find the remainder of $2{,}456{,}789$ divided by $7$.
steps: Since $1001 = 7 \cdot 143$, we have $1000 \equiv -1 \pmod{7}$. So group the digits in threes from the right and alternate signs: $789 - 456 + 2 = 335$.

blocks.html: Starting the alternating sum from the leftmost digit when you want the remainder mod 11. For $4316$: from the right, $6 - 1 + 3 - 4 = 4$, the true remainder ($4316 = 11 \cdot 392 + 4$). From the left, $4 - 3 + 1 - 6 = -4 \equiv 7$, the negative of it. (The two agree when the number has an odd number of digits, or when the answer is 0.) Always give the ones digit the plus sign.

Casting out nines is an old way to check arithmetic: since every number is congruent to its digit sum mod 9, the digit sum of a correct product must match the product of the digit sums, mod 9. It catches most slips, though not swapped digits.
A divisibility test is a congruence for a power of 10: $10 \equiv 1 \pmod{9}$ gives digit sums, and $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$ gives alternating sums from the ones digit.
